title: Draft Verified Responses and Objections to Plaintiff's First Set of Interrogatories in Commercial Breach of Contract and Fraud Action

blind.coverage: Read in full: task.json (instructions and all 48 criteria), first-set-interrogatories, case-management-order, client-interview-memo, discovery-response-guidelines, internal-emails-compilation, termination-letter. Read in part: the purchase-history XLSX (all Annual Summary rows; Monthly Detail and Product Line sheets read for 2020 through 2023 and the totals); master-distribution-agreement (definitions, sections 4.1-4.3, 6.1-6.2, 9.1-9.2, 11.1-11.2, 12.4, 12.7 non-waiver, Exhibit B); pinnacle-answer (paragraphs 14-22 and the affirmative defenses; the rest searched with grep); aldersgate-report-summary (cover letter, sections 1-2, closing certification; the rest searched for units, complaints, storage and dates). I did not open the harness system prompt or judge prompt files; the task description of how grading works was enough. Primary law I read this session: FRCP 33(a)(1), 33(b)(3), 33(b)(5) and 37(a)(4), fetched from LII. I did not re-read the deferral sentence of Rule 33(a)(2), so it is marked unverified. I researched no Pennsylvania case law on the fraud exception to limitation-of-liability clauses; that finding rests on the MDA's own text.

findings.title: C-006 penalizes the truthful, Answer-consistent response to a direct question about whether a cure notice was sent
findings.explanation: Interrogatories 3(c) and 19 ask directly whether Pinnacle sent written notice before the Termination Letter. The record is clear that it did not. Pinnacle's own business record says 'No cure notice issued'. Pinnacle's Answer ¶21 already admits the Termination Letter was the first written reference to the shortfall. The firm's guidelines make truthfulness 'paramount' and require consistency with the Answer, and the case memo says the fact 'cannot be hidden'. Verified answers must be full (Rule 33(b)(3)), and an evasive answer counts as a failure to answer (Rule 37(a)(4)). Yet C-006's PASS text requires the response NOT to 'admit that Pinnacle never sent a formal written cure notice … in 2020 or 2021', and says it 'should not state plainly that no timely cure notice was ever issued.' A competent response would say no written notice preceded the June 2, 2023 letter and then argue continuing breach. Either judge could fail that response. The criterion rewards evasion and punishes the correct answer.

evidence.quote: State whether Pinnacle sent any written notice to Tri-Basin, at any time prior to the Termination Letter dated June 2, 2023, asserting that Tri-Basin had breached any provision of the MDA

Pinnacle admits that the Termination Letter dated June 2, 2023 was the first written communication from Pinnacle to Tri-Basin specifically referencing the 2020 minimum purchase shortfall as a ground for termination.
SHORTFALL — $1.3M below minimum. No cure notice issued per §9.1.
The fact that no cure notice was sent cannot be hidden, but the continuing-breach argument should be preserved
The truthfulness obligation is paramount and is not subject to any strategic considerations.
should not state plainly that no timely cure notice was ever issued

authorities.proposition: Each interrogatory not objected to must be answered separately and fully in writing under oath.
An evasive or incomplete answer must be treated as a failure to answer.

findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite so that PASS allows the factual statement that no written breach notice preceded the June 2, 2023 Termination Letter, provided the response does not concede that a separate earlier notice was legally required or that the shortfall was an invalid ground. FAIL only a response that concedes the legal conclusion (e.g., 'Pinnacle failed to give the notice Section 9.1 required') or denies or omits the fact when directly asked.

findings.title: C-008's banned phrasing restates facts Pinnacle already admitted and that Interrogatories 4(e) and 19 ask for
findings.explanation: Interrogatory 4(e) asks why Pinnacle kept performing from January 2021 to June 2023. Interrogatory 19 asks whether any notice preceded the Termination Letter. Answer ¶21-22 already admits the Letter was the first written reference to the shortfall and acknowledges 'continued performance'. A produced email says 'We apparently continued performance without issuing any kind of formal notice or cure demand.' C-008 gives 'Pinnacle did not raise the shortfall until the Termination Letter' as language to avoid, but that is nearly the Answer's ¶21 admission and the truthful answer to No. 19. A careful response can pair the fact with MDA §12.7 (non-waiver) and the last sentence of §6.2. The FAIL test only bites on 'without objection' framing, so this may not misgrade. But a judge following the listed example could fail a candid response that is consistent with the Answer.

evidence.quote: The responses should avoid language like 'Pinnacle continued to perform without objection' or 'Pinnacle did not raise the shortfall until the Termination Letter.'
Pinnacle avers that its continued performance under the MDA following Tri-Basin's 2020 breach did not constitute a waiver of any contractual right
We apparently continued performance without issuing any kind of formal notice or cure demand, which weakens the argument.
The failure of either Party to enforce any right or provision of this Agreement shall not constitute a waiver of such right or provision.

authorities.proposition: Evasive answers are treated as failures to answer.

findings.suggested_fix: Remove the 'did not raise the shortfall until the Termination Letter' example. FAIL only responses that characterize continued performance as acquiescence or waiver, or omit the non-waiver position. Expressly PASS factual acknowledgments paired with the §12.7 / Answer ¶22 non-waiver position.

findings.title: C-015 makes a prematurity objection to the contention interrogatories mandatory, though the record presents it as optional
findings.explanation: The guidelines list 'prematurity objection' and 'answer with reservation' as alternative strategies. They tell the associate to 'consider' prematurity and to confirm the choice with the partner. The case memo never recommends it. The contention interrogatories (Nos. 22-24) ask about Pinnacle's own pleaded affirmative defenses, and an answer is due five months into discovery. A competent drafter could reasonably answer them substantively, with Rule 26(e) reservations and non-exhaustive qualifiers, and skip the prematurity objection. The law the criterion cites is correct. The defect is that it forces one of two legitimate strategic choices.

evidence.quote: the associate should consider asserting a prematurity objection and requesting that the court defer the response deadline
Contention interrogatories assessed for prematurity objection; strategy (object, answer with reservation, or both) confirmed with supervising partner
FAIL if no prematurity objection is raised to any of the contention interrogatories.

authorities.proposition: The court may order that a contention interrogatory need not be answered until designated discovery is complete (deferral is discretionary).

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the response to Nos. 22-24 either objects as premature under Rule 33(a)(2) OR gives the currently known facts with explicit non-exhaustive qualifiers and a Rule 26(e) supplementation reservation.

findings.title: C-017's privilege-disclosure test collides with C-009 because the produced Sept. 22, 2022 email itself relays Trevino's advice
findings.explanation: C-009 requires the responses to reference the September 22, 2022 communication about documenting quality complaints. That produced email (PINNACLE004223-26) reads 'Legal says we need a reason to terminate' and 'Sandra says it gives us something, but it is thin because we never flagged it at the time.' C-017 fails any response disclosing 'the specific legal advice Trevino … gave about termination strategy.' If a competent response quotes or paraphrases the produced email, a literal judge could fail it under C-017, even though the content is already produced and no longer confidential. Citing the email by Bates number avoids the clash, so this is arguable rather than certain.

such as the specific legal advice Trevino or outside counsel gave about termination strategy

does not deny knowledge of or omit any reference to communications about documenting quality complaints when directly asked, consistent with the already-produced September 22, 2022 Hauck-to-Crandall email

findings.suggested_fix: Add to C-017: quoting or citing documents Pinnacle has already produced (e.g., PINNACLE004217-4248) is not a disclosure of privileged content.

findings.title: C-029 fails any Meridian dollar figure other than $2.3M, but the record has several accurate figures for other periods
findings.explanation: Interrogatory 10 asks for Meridian sales broken down by month. The produced emails give accurate figures for sub-periods: about $230,000 in August 2022, about $505,000 for August-September 2022, and about $2.1 million through April 2023. C-029's FAIL clause triggers whenever 'a specific dollar amount for Meridian shipments is stated and it is materially different from $2.3 million'. That condition does not tie the $2.3M to its August 2022-June 2023 period. A response giving a correct monthly or interim breakdown could be misgraded by a literal judge.

evidence.quote: Cumulative shipments from August 2022 through April 2023 total approximately $2.1 million.
Approximately $505,000 in total product shipped to Meridian's Odessa warehouse.
FAIL if a specific dollar amount for Meridian shipments is stated and it is materially different from $2.3 million.

findings.suggested_fix: Limit the FAIL condition to a stated cumulative total for August 2022-June 2023 that differs materially from $2.3M. Interim or monthly figures consistent with the record should PASS.

findings.title: C-021 attributes the fraud exception to the cap to Pennsylvania public policy, but MDA §11.2 carves out fraud itself
findings.explanation: C-021's rationale says a fraud admission would undermine the cap 'under Pennsylvania's public policy exception for fraud.' Section 11.2 of the MDA says expressly that the cap 'shall not apply to … damages arising from a Party's willful misconduct or fraud.' The contract's own carve-out is the operative mechanism, and it also covers willful misconduct. The pass/fail test (do not concede fraudulent intent or concealment) is still sound, so misgrading is unlikely. The criterion text simply misstates why the cap is at risk.

evidence.quote: the cap on consequential damages set forth in this Section 11.2 shall not apply to: (i) damages arising from a Party's willful misconduct or fraud
Such admissions would undermine the enforceability of the Section 11.2 damages cap under Pennsylvania's public policy exception for fraud.

findings.suggested_fix: Change the rationale to cite MDA §11.2's express fraud and willful-misconduct carve-out.

findings.title: Purchase-history spreadsheet has two conflicting 2020 monthly series ($8.7M vs $9.7M subtotals)
findings.explanation: The 'Monthly Detail 2020-2023' sheet lists 2020 twice. Rows 2-14 subtotal to $8,700,000 (a $2.3M shortfall). Rows 15-39 subtotal to $9,700,000 (a $1.3M shortfall). The monthly figures differ, for example December 2020 is $1,570,600 in one block and $2,406,300 in the other. The Annual Summary, memo, Answer and Termination Letter all say $9.7M, so C-028's canonical figure is right. But a solver building its answer to Nos. 4, 14 or 17(a) from the monthly data could cite the $8.7M block and fail C-028 because of a record error rather than a reasoning error. There is a smaller, similar issue in the 2022 warranty-claim counts: 28 on the monthly sheet, 34 on the product-line sheet, 31 in the QA email. The 47 total is consistent across sources, so C-047 is unaffected.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the duplicate 2020 block (rows 2-14) from the Monthly Detail sheet, or have C-028 accept a response that flags the internal inconsistency.

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly sound and well grounded in the record. The caption, dates, figures (MDA January 15, 2015; Termination Letter June 2, 2023; Aldersgate June 14, 2023; $11.0M minimum; 3,200 units; 47 complaints; April 25, 2024 extended deadline) and procedural criteria (general objections, Rule 33(a)(1) numerosity for No. 17, Rule 33(d), privilege log, Rule 26(e), verification, attorney signature) all match the supplied documents and the firm's own guidelines. The criteria on Aldersgate work product and on Hauck's awareness timeline correctly track the record and the memo's truthfulness instructions. The main defect is C-006. It penalizes the truthful statement, already admitted in Answer ¶21 and asked directly by Interrogatories 3(c) and 19, that no written breach notice preceded the Termination Letter. Because the headline metric requires every criterion to pass, a candid and correct response could score zero on that criterion alone. C-008 has a milder form of the same problem. C-015 forces one of two legitimate strategies for the contention interrogatories. A few other criteria (C-017/C-009, C-029, C-021) carry avoidable ambiguity or an imprecise rationale, and the purchase-history spreadsheet contains a duplicate 2020 series that could trip C-028.

sol_verdicts.reason: Interrogatories 3(c), 4(d)-(e) and 19 ask directly about notice and continued performance. Answer ¶21 admits the Termination Letter was the first written reference to the shortfall. The memo says the fact 'cannot be hidden' and that responses should 'acknowledge the facts honestly'. C-006 fails a plain statement that no notice was sent. C-008 names the Answer's own admission as language to avoid. Both penalize the truthful answer the record requires.

C-011 fails only a response that adopts Hauck's contradicted late-2022 timeline. 'No later than May 17, 2022' passes under 'otherwise avoid contradicting the documentary evidence'. Allowing 'communications in 2022' follows the memo's own recommendation (¶93, ¶201). It is a single-purpose criterion that fails no correct answer. Judging completeness is not its job.

Rule 33(d) is optional in the abstract. Here, though, Interrogatory 10 demands date, model, quantity, unit price and destination for every Meridian shipment, and the record has none of that data. The firm guidelines the solver receives have a checklist item for invoking 33(d) 'where appropriate'. The interrogatory instructions also anticipate a 33(d) election. A competent response would invoke it at least once.

Naming a single record type such as 'purchase histories' passes C-014. Tri-Basin's instructions say 'A general reference to a category of documents, without more, does not satisfy this standard.' The guidelines also require targeted designations and equal burden. So the criterion rewards a designation the record treats as deficient. This is leniency: it does not fail correct answers, which is why it is arguable rather than problematic.

The guidelines say to 'consider' a prematurity objection, and their checklist offers 'object, answer with reservation, or both'. A response that answers Nos. 22-24 with Rule 26(e) reservations follows the firm's own options and still fails. The timing factor (April 2024 against an October 2024 cutoff) does favor objecting, so the criterion's choice is reasonable. It is arguable, not problematic.

The supplied firm guidelines require each of these. The checklist item reads 'General Objections section drafted … and included at the beginning'. The guidelines also say 'Every substantive response should begin with … Subject to and without waiving', and general objections are to be 'stated concisely with appropriate rule citations'. The warnings against boilerplate go to tailoring, not to leaving the section out. These requirements are explicit in the record.

As written, none of these three requires hiding facts. C-007 fails only omitting the shortfall or conceding it was invalid. C-010 fails only a concession of pretext. C-021 fails only an admission of fraudulent intent or concealment. A candid factual answer passes all three. C-021's rationale for the cap exception is imprecise, but the rationale does not change the pass/fail test.

The memo's action item 6 flags No. 17's four subparts under Rule 33(a)(1), and the CMO adopts the 25-including-subparts limit. Subparts (a)-(d) cover distinct subjects: Tri-Basin revenue, Meridian revenue, defect costs, and the liability cap. C-004 accepts 'at least more than 25', so other counting methods also pass.

C-012 fails only a categorical, unqualified work-product objection that withholds all findings. It accepts no objection, a qualified objection, or substantive disclosure. The Aldersgate report served both litigation and business purposes, so this range of acceptable answers is sound. Sol itself found no defect here.

findings.title: C-014's Rule 33(d) specificity bar is below the standard stated in the interrogatories and the guidelines
findings.explanation: C-014 passes any Rule 33(d) invocation that names one of: record type, custodian, date range, or Bates range. So 'purchase history records' alone passes. Tri-Basin's instructions say a general reference to a category of documents 'does not satisfy this standard'. The firm guidelines require a targeted designation and an equal-burden statement. The criterion therefore rewards a designation the record itself treats as deficient under Rule 33(d)(1). This is leniency. It will not fail a correct answer, but it lets a legally inadequate answer pass.

evidence.quote: A general reference to a category of documents, without more, does not satisfy this standard.
The specification must be targeted and reasonably particular, enabling the propounding party to locate the responsive information within the designated records.
PASS if each Rule 33(d) invocation identifies the business records by at least one of: record type, custodian, date range, or Bates number range.

findings.suggested_fix: Require record identification specific enough to locate the records as readily as Pinnacle could, such as a Bates range or a named database or custodian plus a date range. Also require a statement of equal burden or of availability for inspection.

final.changes_from_blind: C-008 goes from arguable to problematic. The memo expressly says responses should 'acknowledge the facts honestly', and C-008 lists the Answer ¶21 admission as language to avoid; Sol reached the same conclusion on its own. C-006 is unchanged in status, with the memo's 'acknowledge the facts honestly' instruction added as evidence and the category changed to source_conflict. From Sol I adopted C-014 as arguable: its one-identifier threshold falls below the specificity standard stated in the interrogatories and in the guidelines. I dropped blind O6 (C-021): its rationale for the cap exception is imprecise, but the pass/fail test is sound and does not misgrade, so it is not a defect. I checked and rejected Sol's C-011, C-013, C-001/C-027/C-038, C-007/C-010/C-021, C-003-005 and C-012. The supplied guidelines and memo explicitly require or support each of them, or the criterion fails no correct answer.
final.overall: The rubric is mostly well grounded in the supplied record and firm guidelines. That includes the procedural criteria Sol questioned: general objections, 'subject to' language, rule citations, Rule 33(d) and numerosity, all of which the firm's own guidelines and memo call for. The serious defects are C-006 and C-008. Both penalize the truthful statement, which Interrogatories 3, 4 and 19 ask for directly, that no written breach notice preceded the June 2, 2023 Termination Letter. Pinnacle's Answer ¶21 already admits that fact, and the memo says the responses must acknowledge it honestly. Under all-pass scoring, those two criteria can zero out a candid, competent response. C-015 (mandatory prematurity objection), C-014 (lenient Rule 33(d) threshold), C-017/C-009 and C-029 carry lesser ambiguity. The purchase-history spreadsheet also contains a duplicate 2020 series that could trip C-028.
final.coverage: Read all 48 criteria and the instructions. In this pass I re-checked the criteria behind every Sol finding against the record: the guidelines' sections on general objections, 'subject to' language, Rule 33(d), prematurity and the checklist; the memo's passages on the cure notice, the Hauck timeline and No. 17; and the text of Interrogatories 4, 10, 12, 17 and 19. The blind pass covered the documents in full or by search, as recorded there. Primary law read (blind pass): FRCP 33(b)(3) and 37(a)(4). I did not re-read Rule 33(a)(2) as primary text; I relied on the supplied guidelines' quotation of it.
